title: How many clocks does China need?
hook: China is as wide as four hours of sunlight. Check what its clocks say.

knows: that the world has time zones
that the Sun is highest around noon
doesNotKnow: that time zones are set by law, not by geometry
how far clock time can drift from Sun time

misconception: A country as wide as China has several time zones, and clock time tracks the Sun.
objective: The learner can explain that China uses one official time, UTC+8, so in the far west the Sun is highest around 3 p.m. on the clock, and that time zones are decisions rather than geometry.

claims.text: China uses one official standard time, Beijing time, UTC+8.
claims.source: IANA tz database (zone1970.tab: Asia/Shanghai for most of China, UTC+08 with no DST since 1991). Asia/Urumqi (UTC+06) is listed for local usage in Xinjiang; the lesson says 'official standard time' and makes no claim about local conventions. Not opened by the builder (network blocked).

claims.text: China spans about 61° of longitude, roughly 4 hours of the Sun's travel.
claims.source: Kit 1:110m 'China' outline: 73.68 E to 135.02 E, 61.35 degrees; 61.35 / 15 = 4.09 h (artifacts/scratch/w1-misc.mjs; computed live in Demo.tsx). The outline makes no border claim.

claims.text: On the official clock the Sun is highest over Kashgar at about 14:56, nearly 3 p.m., and over Shanghai at about 11:54.
claims.source: Mean solar noon at longitude L is 12:00 UTC - L/15 h; plus 8 h. Kashgar 75.99 E: 14:56; Shanghai 121.47 E: 11:54. Gazetteer coordinates (GeoNames) not opened. The equation of time shifts real solar noon by up to about 16 minutes (c4).

claims.text: The real Sun runs up to about 16 minutes early or late during the year compared with mean Sun time.
claims.source: Equation of time, range about -14 to +16 minutes (Astronomical Almanac; Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms ch. 28).

claims.text: The Sun's noon moves 15° of longitude per hour, so 15° bands are what geometry alone would suggest for time zones.
claims.source: 360 degrees / 24 h = 15 degrees per hour. The dashed lines are nominal bands centred on multiples of 15 degrees (edges at 67.5, 82.5, ... 142.5 E), not legal zones; the stage caption says '15° bands'.

claims.text: A time zone is a decision made by law, not a line drawn by the Sun.
claims.source: Time zones are set by national governments (e.g. IANA tz database notes; Wikipedia 'Time zone'). Framing claim.

recall.question: In western China the clock reads 15:00. Roughly where is the Sun?
options: Low in the west, near sunset
Close to its highest point of the day
recall.why: All of China keeps UTC+8, which fits the east; in the far west the Sun reaches its highest point around 3 p.m. on that clock.
